E DIN EN 61131-10:2017-11

Nationales Vorworte

Die englische Originalfassung des internationalen Dokuments IEC 65B/1070/CD:2017 „Programmable
controllers – Part 10: XML Exchange Formats for Programs according to IEC 61131-3“ (CD, en: Committee
Draft) ist unverändert in diesen Norm-Entwurf übernommen worden. Dieser Norm-Entwurf enthält eine
autorisierte deutsche Übersetzung.

Das internationale Dokument wurde vom SC 65B „Measurement and control devices“ der Internationalen
Elektrotechnischen Kommission (IEC) erarbeitet und den nationalen Komitees zur Stellungnahme vorgelegt.

Die IEC und das Europäische Komitee für Elektrotechnische Normung (CENELEC) haben vereinbart, dass
ein auf IEC-Ebene erarbeiteter Entwurf für eine Internationale Norm zeitgleich (parallel) bei IEC und
CENELEC zur Umfrage (CDV-Stadium) und Abstimmung als FDIS (en: Final Draft International Standard)
bzw. Schluss-Entwurf für eine Europäische Norm gestellt wird, um eine Beschleunigung und Straffung der
Normungsarbeit zu erreichen. Dokumente, die bei CENELEC als Europäische Norm angenommen und ratifiziert werden, sind unverändert als Deutsche Normen zu übernehmen.

Da der Abstimmungszeitraum für einen FDIS bzw. Schluss-Entwurf prEN nur 2 Monate beträgt, und dann
keine sachlichen Stellungnahmen mehr abgegeben werden können, sondern nur noch eine „JA/NEIN“-Entscheidung möglich ist, wobei eine „NEIN“-Entscheidung fundiert begründet werden muss, wird bereits der
CD als DIN-Norm-Entwurf veröffentlicht, um die Stellungnahmen aus der Öffentlichkeit frühzeitig berücksichtigen zu können.

Für dieses Dokument ist das nationale Arbeitsgremium K 962 „SPS“ der DKE Deutsche Kommission Elektrotechnik Elektronik Informationstechnik in DIN und VDE (www.dke.de) zuständig.

Für den Fall einer undatierten Verweisung im normativen Text (Verweisung auf ein Dokument ohne Angabe
des Ausgabedatums und ohne Hinweis auf eine Abschnittsnummer, eine Tabelle, ein Bild usw.) bezieht sich
die Verweisung auf die jeweils aktuellste Ausgabe des in Bezug genommenen Dokuments.

Für den Fall einer datierten Verweisung im normativen Text bezieht sich die Verweisung immer auf die in
Bezug genommene Ausgabe des Dokuments.

Der Zusammenhang der zitierten Dokumente mit den entsprechenden Deutschen Dokumenten ergibt sich,
soweit ein Zusammenhang besteht, grundsätzlich über die Nummer der entsprechenden IEC-Publikation.
Beispiel: IEC 60068 ist als EN 60068 als Europäische Norm durch CENELEC übernommen und als
DIN EN 60068 ins Deutsche Normenwerk aufgenommen.

Das Präsidium des DIN hat mit Präsidialbeschluss 1/2004 festgelegt, dass DIN-Normen, deren Inhalt sich auf
internationale Arbeitsergebnisse der Informationsverarbeitung gründet, unter bestimmten Bedingungen allein
in englischer Sprache veröffentlicht werden dürfen. Diese Bedingungen sind für den vorliegenden Normentwurf erfüllt.

Da sich die Benutzer des vorliegenden Normentwurfs der englischen Sprache als Fachsprache bedienen,
wird die Englische Fassung der EN 61131-10 veröffentlicht. Zu deren Abschnitt 1 und Abschnitt 3, der die
Begriffe festlegt, wurde eine Übersetzung angefertigt und als informativer Nationaler Anhang NA des vorliegenden Normentwurfs hinzugefügt. Für viele der verwendeten Begriffe existieren keine gebräuchlichen deutschen Benennungen, da sich die deutschen Anwender in der Regel ebenfalls der englischen Benennungen
bedienen. Dieser Normentwurf steht nicht in unmittelbarem Zusammenhang mit Rechtsvorschriften und ist
nicht als Sicherheitsnorm anzusehen.

Es wird auf die Möglichkeit hingewiesen, dass einige Elemente dieses Dokuments Patentrechte berühren
können. ISO [und/oder] IEC sind nicht dafür verantwortlich, einige oder alle diesbezüglichen Patentrechte zu
identifizieren.

Die vorliegende Norm enthält keine Anforderungen an die übereinstimmenden Funktionen der PUTE. Sie legt
ein Austauschformat für den Austausch von Programmen fest, die mit IEC 61131-3 übereinstimmen.

**3** **Begriffe und Abkürzungen**

**3.1** **Allgemeine Begriffe**

Für die Anwendung dieses Dokuments gelten die in IEC 61131-3 angegebenen und die folgenden Begriffe.

**3.1.1**
**IEC 61131-3-Projekt**

有很大的改善空间。This standard specifies an XML-based exchange format for the export and import of IEC 61131-3 projects. A complete IEC 61131-3 project implemented in an IEC 61131-3 environment can be transferred between different programming environments. It allows for the exchange of configuration elements, data types, and POUs written in:

- the textual language, Instruction List (IL),
- the textual language, Structured Text (ST),
- the graphical language, Ladder Diagram (LD),
- the graphical language, Function Block Diagram (FBD), and
- Sequential Function Chart (SFC).

The exchange format is specified as a corresponding XML schema. The XML schema is an independent file with the .xsd extension and as such part of this specification. A description of this schema is contained in this standard. It is assumed that the reader of this standard is familiar with XML technology.

Figure 1 provides an example overview of the usage of the XML exchange format. Different tools are producing and consuming XML based IEC 61131-3 information.

The use of the XML exchange format should provide more than a simple export / import from one development environment to another. All relevant information should be exported. This may include coordinate information for graphical tools. The importing tool should be able to filter which parts of this information need to be imported into its destination environment. Vendor specific information and attributes may be included in the export file and selectively imported, if applicable. The vendor specific information shall not influence the logic part of the program. Filtering should be done on the import – thus vendors shall take care that their extensions of the XML schema shall be done in such a way that neglecting the information

### Page 16

)}

The described formats are designed for the import and export of IEC 61131-3 project. Such an IEC 61131-3 project can be under development and as a consequence incomplete.

Concerning the exchange of graphical language constructs between different Programming Systems, the focus is on logical information with optional explicit graphics.

1.2 Implementation Specific Parameters

This standard does not provide means or requirements for compliant functionality (e.g. functional subset which has to be supported by all Programming and Debugging Tools (PADTs)). This standard enables the exchange of all possible features defined in IEC 61131-3. Moreover, many implementation specific features can be expressed using the AddData mechanism.

In some use cases programs are either transferred from one PADT to another or generated for the use in different PADT. In both cases the function set of these PADT may be different as well as their settings of implementation dependent parameters. If several PADT have to be supported/considered, the functionality of the program has to be restricted to the subset supported by all PADTs in question. Some of these functions can be determined from the IEC 61131-3 feature tables of the concerned PADT, for example:

• supported data types and standard functions,
• pre-emptive or non-pre-emptive scheduling,
• SFC with or without a final scan, etc.

Other functions and settings of implementation dependent parameters may require more effort to determine, for example:

• maximum amounts of code or variables per POU,
• maximum length of identifiers (variable name length),
• size of STRING and WSTRING variables with default length or maximum length,
• SFC to evaluate all transition conditions or only those with active steps as predecessors,
• range and precision of data types TIME, DATE, TOD, DT,
• runtime performance of (the POU in) the PLC,
• execution order within a graphical network, etc.

These differences have to be considered for use cases with more than one PADT. In some cases it may be appropriate to use only functionality supported by all concerned PADTs, in other cases it may be necessary to manually change and test the program after importing into the PADT.

This standard does not state requirements regarding compliant functions of the PADT. It defines an exchange format to exchange programs which are compliant to IEC 61131-3.

2 Normative references

The following documents, in whole or in part, are normatively referenced in this standard and are indispensable for its application. For dated references, only the edition cited applies. For undated references, the latest edition of the referenced document (including any amendments) applies.

IEC 61131-1, Programmable controllers – Part 1: General information

IEC 61131-3, Programmable controllers – Part 3: Programming Languages}

selected articles:

1. [Figure 23 — Complex type "TextualObjectBase"](#)
   - **Description:**
     - The figure represents an object "TextualObjectBase" with the ID and attributes such as TextualObjectBase, attributes (text), pragma, usingDirective.

2. **Figure 24 — Complex type "NamespaceContentBase"**
   - **Description:**
     - The figure illustrates an object "NamespaceContentBase" which is based on the abstract type "TextualObjectBase". It includes the namespace content of the object including its type and the namespaces it comprises.

3. **TextualObjectBase (Extension)**
   - **Description:**
     - The figure shows an extension to the "TextualObjectBase" interface "TextualObjectBase".
     - It has attributes: TextualObjectBase, attributes, pragma, usingDirective.
     - The "TextualObjectBase" is marked as a subtype of "NamespaceContentBase", indicating that it makes any of the commoners (TextualObjectBase) and marks all the other as the specific ones (NamespaceContentBase).
     - Attributes include namespaces, programmer-defined object base, and empty namespace.

4. **NamespaceContentBase (Extension)**
   - **Description:**
     - The figure defines the "NamespaceContentBase" as an additional type with all the commoners missing and making all the specific types defined in the base.
     - It is extended only by attributes: NamespaceBase, attributes, name, internal, and forms a separate base for namespace content.

5. **Diagram 23:**
   - **Description:**
     - Illustrates the previous definitions with an "Attribute" representing an attribute to its namespace in "Understanding PowerShell Objects" book.
     - The attribute "pragma" represents the type string.

6. **Diagram 24:**
   - **Description:**
     - Shows the hierarchy extension for a simple "Object" from "Microsoft PowerShell 5.1 documentation" with the "NamespaceContentBase" and the attributes string.
     - An enum is not shown but leaves implementaion in words.

These diagrams collectively outline the structure and hierarchical relationships between different objects and types in the PowerShell API, specifically the NamespaceContentExtensions and NamespaceContentBase.

A "UserDefinedTypeDecl" inherits all elements of the type "NamespaceContentBase"This is an alphabetized list of items in a sequence, starting with A and ending with Z. Each item is identified by a letter or uppercase word followed by a number in parentheses.

\sqrt{G}\) is introduced to represent the square root of a number. The number in the braces can be either a small or capital letter as per the requirement.

Figure 27 lists the supported data types of array data types, and the indexing flags for subclauses that define arrays of the NativeBase types. Most of the base types in the array data types are defined with the ability to store any data type.

value length.The figure illustrates the mapping process between CD 61131-10 and its corresponding EDI file, as described in the paper "Level-Sensitive Analysis of EDI." The relationship between the CD 61131-10 and the EDI file is denoted by different connections such as "AttrId," "typName," "varAttr," "edge," and "suppressName." Each connection has a specific role in the EDI data structure, and the figure shows how these connections are mapped to specific elements in the EDI file.

Here is a detailed description of the mapping process for the figure:

1. **AttrId Connection:**
   - **AttrId:** The first attribute in the CD 61131-10 is connected to the CD 61131-10 "AttrId" element in the EDI file.
   - **TypName:** The next attribute in the CD 61131-10 is associated with the element named "typName," which maps to the "alias" of the attribute in the EDI file.
   - **VarAttr:** The third attribute in the CD 61131-10 is related to the element named "varAttr," which corresponds to the "data" or "instance" of the attribute in the EDI file.
   - **Edge:** The attribute "edge" in the CD 61131-10 is tied to the "edge" element in the EDI file.
   - **SuppressName:** The fourth attribute in the CD 61131-10 is connected to the "suppressName" element in the EDI file.

2. **Block, TypeName, and InstanceName Connections:**
   - **Block:** The "block" connection in the CD 61131-10 is mapped to the "Block" element in the EDI file. This indicates that the block component of the CD 61131-10 is represented as a block in the EDI file.
   - **TypeName:** The "typeName" connection in the CD 61131-10 is associated with the "TypName" element in the EDI file, which maps to the "TYPE" in the EDI.
   - **InstanceName:** The "instanceName" connection in the CD 61131-10 is linked to the "InstanceName" element in the EDI file, which maps to the "INSTANCE" in the EDI.

3. **Input Output Variables Connections:**
   - **AttrId Input Variables:** The "attrIdInputVariables" connection in the CD 61131-10 is mapped to the "InputVariables" element in the EDI file. This indicates that the input variables for the attribute "attrId" are represented as part of the "inputVariables" element in the EDI.
   - **Data Input Variables:** Another "inputVariables" connection in the CD 61131-10 is mapped to the "InputVariables" element in the EDI, indicating that the data variable for the attribute "typName" is part of the "inputVariables" element in the EDI.

4. **Output Variables Connections:**
   - **AttrId Output Variables:** The "attrIdOutputVariables" connection in the CD 61131-10 is associated with the "OutputVariables" element in the EDI, representing the output variables for the attribute "attrId."
   - **Data Output Variables:** A "outputVariables" connection in the CD 61131-10 is linked to the "OutputVariables" element in the EDI, indicating that the output variable for the attribute "typeName" is part of the "outputVariables" element in the EDI.

5. **Info Line Connections:**
   - The "infoLine" connections in the CD 61131-10 are mapped to the "infoLine" elements in the EDI. These "infoLine" elements likely represent additional information or annotations associated with the attributes or instances.

Overall, the figure provides a comprehensive view of how the different connection elements in the CD 61131-10 map to elements in the EDI file, illustrating the level-sensitive mapping process from the concept level to the data level.

The abstract summarizes the content of the research paper, which aims to describe string matching in databases and develop a regular expression editor. It highlights the significance of the project in improving the ease and process of database searches.
**Introduction**:
The introduction connects the abstract to the broader context of the research, noting the importance of regular expressions and editors in database management. It mentions that the Editor uses a graphical representation of value assignments to facilitate the search for patterns in strings.
**Related Work**:
The related work section discusses the limitations of existing systems, such as FdbObjectBase, and proposes improvements. It states that the new system is expected to be more efficient and user-friendly.
**Methodology**:
The methodology details the software architecture and the design of the graphical representation tools. It briefly mentions the use of action maps and the role of various components in the system.
**Experiences**:
Participants are invited to the meeting for further questions and additional information.
**Conclusion**:
The editor is developed to offer a visual representation of variable values and to simplify the complex process of pattern matching in databases. The project is expected to be useful for database developers and researchers.

“ConnectionPointIn” of type “ConnectionPointIn” and “ConnectionPointOut” of type

“ConnectionPointOut” are explained in the sub-clauses 13.5.1 and 13.5.4.

13.5 Connections

13.5.1 General

A “Connection” expresses the connection between 2 graphical objects. The source object has
a “ConnectionPointOut” and the sink object has a “ConnectionPointIn”. The connection itself
is always specified at the “ConnectionPointIn”. If several sources are connected to the same
sink (e.g. several contacts to one coil in LD) then a collection of “Connection” is specified at
the “ConnectionPointIn”.

Each “ConnectionPointOut” has an attribute “connectionPointOutId” which shall be unique
within each “Body”. The “Connection” at the “ConnectionPointIn” has an attribute
“refConnectionPointOutId” which refers to the “connectionPointOutId” of the corresponding
“ConnectionPointOut”.

13.5.2 “ConnectionPointIn”

The complex type “ConnectionPointIn” represents the incoming connection point necessary to
realize a predecessor-successor relationship. Its content is shown in Figure 84.

Figure 84 – Complex type “ConnectionPointIn”

As a result an initial menu of ten topics is presented in Figure 35. The emphasis in the list of existing variables is that most are defined in the "Domain Domain" sub-library instead of their base physical location; at the same time, as key terms (and often references to conceptual qualities) are not self-contained units, this means additional information must be obtained from other sources.

Figure 36 shows the programme descriptions (but the descriptions of the types covered are shown in the Outer Roads descriptions found in Topic 28). The Program descriptions have been presented without the subdivision into little sections, but the creation of specific sub-libraries for these has been deleted due to the limitations on the display of specific symbols.

The programme description takes the shape given by it being a pseudocode description of one or more execution sequences that could be carried out by the sub-programme indicated in the description; the actual nature and implementation details of the programme are beyond the scope of this particular document.

There are three main points to make with regard to the program descriptions. First, the organisation of the description has been done in such a way that the reader should be able to follow the programme development process. However, there are a number of difficulties in this approach: not only will the defining of these algorithms be more difficult than you might be expecting, but the fact that we merely describe the outlines of the real message at the time of specification means that these descriptions have been does retain a description of the later specified subtractions, and is also a bit misleading in regard to the general nature of the information. Second, describing the programme execution is a much more difficult matter than the defining of the objector's messages or, indeed, this (ie the process of describing a program plan containing methods and parameters).

The third point to make is that the specification will be written using technical "best practice". The use of "technical" will be understood to mean "sound" - in terms of both consistency, and, significantly, "correctness" in the view of efficient formalisation of decision criteria. However, this should not be interpreted as "poor technical practice" or implying that all specifications should be exact mathematical theorems - on the contrary, the intention is that they will (at least to some degree) include all the practical issues based on clearly defined criteria for selection.

One further caveat is worth making concerning the representation of elaborations in the case of different sub-programmes; even if the language is only intended for programming, then one should expect some documentation for the objectives and format required to capture these details, although it is certainly true as per suggested text that these high level document types have only recently been specified (as we have also seen in the description of the "Standard UML" standard). The planning and operator description techniques are considerably longer as a single unit, but in respect to tailoring for generic documentation it is anticipated that these will take longer to specify than the low level ones. The reason for this is that although modelling aids unique solutions (eg. models for proposal or needs) have been developed at each level, in practice they are used only wherever required unless the subprogramme is so complicated that it might be necessary for this "style" to be employed; in that case, such terms are more apt to have some value.

Flipkart initially ventured into the unit costs of e-commerce, but its approach to reducing unit costs over time led it to focus on unit formats, shipping, and labor costs instead. With this change, the company would be one of the first e-commerce players to devote a significant portion of its workforce to operating costs rather than customer-facing product downloads.\n\n> $title> Rolling out fixed costs without reducing customer-facing units is not sustainable for e-commerce
At e-commerce's launch, a 10,000-store e-tail business, there were no fixed expenses \textit{{such as unit costs}}. By contrast, the vanily launched e-commerce business with only 20,000 outlets and 550,000 customers: typical costs, equipment, and labor for unstructured, online customer visits.\n\nThe traditional way to reduce costs is to cut average order size and/or customer visits without reducing the total amount of revenue in the global revenue stream. 首先将 baselist 文件创建在根目录下的命令中。然后，创建一个新的 C# 方法，名称为一个名为 "function" 的类，该类将包含与当前类的所有内容相对应的函数。为了保持代码的简洁，请使用接口或基类的那些约定。

接下来，在文本框中输入品牌名称、产品名称、类型、数字版本、SPCC 文本、自定义文本、基准号、规格和 MSRP（建议价格），然后单击文件按钮添加新内容。文本框中只显示输入的产品属性，不包括其他信息。还可以重新定义分类类型。

然后，在表格中创建 SPCS 标签的另一个新列，并将列名设置为分类编码和名称，如果需要则添加自定义文本。还可以添加基类中非子类进行的相同列。

选择该列为一项学分，最后单击添加按钮。

transition.In this paper, the authors propose a new representation for continuous dependencies between 2D and 3D objects, called “characteristic Over-Segmented Transform” (COTT) dependencies. They also introduce a new method for computing these dependencies in a data efficient manner. The authors benchmarked their representation on three tasks related to 3D object recognition: object classification, obstacle detection, and 3D object pose estimation. On the classification task, the authors achieved impressive results.

The authors of the paper present a new representation of 2D to 3D continuous transformations between objects. Their method combines prior work on 2D-3D correspondence with four new pieces of information. First, they use a method to do interpoint registration from objects in Category (question image) to Category (query image). Corresponding points are then marked for each object. Then, they compute orientation of each point in attibute feet with respect to center of object.

To do inter-transform, they use gradient descent over all possible permutations of transformations.

To compute continuous dependencies, the authors take the following steps:

1. Find correspondence for each object on a dataset. training data set is then numbered, and computed correspondence matrices on which of the correspondences thus computed, and find transformation between two hashtags tyrosine tyrosine  on these correspondences.

2. Find Point of Intersection between query wasserstein–Cayley animation from correspondence matrix on transformation and object with transformation found.

3. Compute Tanimoto similarity between two similarity matrix.

4. Compute the average distance of transformation signified by transformation matrix.

     We notice that the calculation is slow for large datasets. So the authors optimization method to solve the problem, and say that the method can boost the performance signification up to 60%.

5. Assign transformation to 2D projections of Unity skeleton of shape class in the query.

The paper includes a comparison with previous work on this topic show that the authors’ method is significantly more accurate. The authors also show that their new representation can be used to solve robot motion planning problems. The paper also includes a paper that is similar to the one above. The authors also refer to other similar papers. The authors also include a reference list.

The WHERE clause is a logical condition that is used to filter the rows that are returned by the SELECT statement. If there are multiple rows that satisfy the condition, the results may not necessarily be sorted or ordered in a predictable manner.

Archaeological surveys give considerable information, such as the description of areas, time of a finds/later activities, and the distinction of objects and activities between layers and regions. They are often used in combination with methodological guides to begin the research process, determine the types of finds and features, and discuss possible indications and periods. Since the end of the 20th century, archaeological surveys have also moved toward accommodating advances in technology and new requirements in such forms of method and of finding ways to improve, to get more productive and positive results,or to produce better ‘social scripts’ by knowing what to find.
